slides.feedback: There is no one shape for a poem. Today we test each idea.
slides.hint: Do not worry about right or wrong. What did you look at?
slides.notes: Sayable: Could this be a poem? Which one is BEST? Silent 10s, gesture vote (fingers 1/2/3), take 3 hands max: What makes you think so? Expect split vote, no-rhyme dominant. OPEN VOTE: renderer needs one canonical; Not sure is a neutral placeholder only — accept all answers, log rhyme-equals-rule misconception, do not correct yet. Bridge: Let's meet a real poet. 1E: accept one-word answers. [ELICIT ~3 min]
slides.prompt: Could this be a poem? Which one is BEST?
slides.stimulus: The rain is falling. The road is wet. People are going home.

visual.alt: Two pupils holding hands together, neutral together-mood

slides.feedback: The subject is ordinary — a child on a swing — but exciting.
slides.hint: Look at the word that comes three times. What is it?
slides.notes: Sayable: Read the two lines. Which one is BEST? Read excerpt aloud twice; pupils repeat second line chorally before voting. Expect near-unanimous B; if journey/dream, note over-inference. Follow-up oral (no writing): Could you write about something ordinary — football, rain, your cat? Collect 4–5 ideas. Bridge: If a swing can be a poem, what about rhyme? [NOTICE ~4 min]
slides.prompt: What is this poem about? Which one is BEST?
slides.stimulus: "How do you like to go up in a swing, Up in the air so blue?" — Robert Louis Stevenson, The Swing

slides.feedback: Some poems rhyme. Some do not. Rhyme is a tool, not a rule.
slides.hint: Say comes. Say feet. Same end sound?
slides.notes: Sayable: Say the last word of each line. Which one is BEST? A/B fingers. Expect fast No; if Yes, say pair aloud once, no phonics lecture. Log rhyme-as-rule. Bridge: If rhyme is not the secret, what makes these lines interesting? [COMPARE ~3 min]
slides.prompt: Does a poem have to rhyme? Which is BEST?
slides.stimulus: The fog comes on little cat feet — from Carl Sandburg, Fog. Do comes and feet rhyme?

slides.hint: Close your eyes. Fog moves. Loud or quiet?
slides.notes: Sayable: What picture do you see in your head? Read aloud once normal, once slowly; point to each line; pupils repeat sits / looks / moves chorally. Accept any visual (cat, smoke, ghost animal). Do NOT define personification yet. Word bank voiceable if stuck: fog, cat feet, sits, looks, moves. Bridge: Fog cannot really sit. So what did the poet do? [NOTICE ~4 min]
slides.prompt: What picture do you see in your head?
slides.text: The fog comes on little cat feet. It sits looking over harbor and city on silent haunches and then moves on. — Carl Sandburg, Fog

slides.feedback: Fog has no feet. The poet gives fog a living action. This is personification.
slides.hint: Does fog have legs? Where did the feet come from?
slides.notes: Sayable: Can fog really have feet? Which one is BEST? After vote show micro-examples orally: The wind whispers. The moon watches. The rain dances. Term pupil wording: personification gives something non-human a human or living action. Try-it oral with frame + bank (sleeps / waits / smiles): The door ___ . The sun ___ . Accept any living-action verb. Misconception: poem must be literally true. Bridge: Poets also choose small exact words. [EXPLAIN ~4 min]
slides.prompt: Fog has feet. True or impossible? Which is BEST?
slides.stimulus: The fog comes on little cat feet.

slides.answer: Cold rain taps on my window
slides.feedback: B uses specific words — cold, taps, window — so you see and hear it.
slides.hint: Which one can you see and hear? Which words help?
slides.notes: Sayable: Which one is BEST — A or B? Key line: Specific words make pictures. Counter long-word myth: Did B use difficult English? No — exact English. Try-it oral with frame: The dog ___ . (sleeps / waits / barks / watches). Accept any specific verb. Bridge: Now watch one plain sentence become a poem. [COMPARE ~4 min]
options: Cold rain taps on my window
slides.prompt: Which one gives you a clearer picture? Which is BEST?
slides.stimulus: A. The rain is nice. B. Cold rain taps on my window.

items: The loud school bell shouts through the tired afternoon.
slides.notes: Sayable per step: What can we add? What stronger verb? Where does it shout? Build orally BEFORE revealing each line; offer verb choices (rings / shouts / sings) rather than open elicitation. Accept variants (cries, hot evening). Say: We did not need difficult English. Summary: detail, strong verb, image. Bridge: Those moves have names. [MODEL ~4 min]
slides.prompt: How can we make this more interesting?
Your poet's toolbox — five choices. You need one.
slides.text: 1. Specific words — cold rain taps. 2. Simile — moon like a lamp. 3. Personification — wind whispers. 4. Repetition — I wait, I wait. 5. Line breaks — rain / falls / tonight.
slides.notes: SYNTHESIS REFERENCE (~3 min, no new teaching, nothing hidden). All five visible from the start. Point to each; pupils repeat each example chorally. Point back: 1 = rain, 2-4 just now, 5 = bell break. Sayable: Poetry is making choices with ordinary words. Bridge: Now test yourself — which tool is this?

slides.feedback: The moon cannot smile. The poet gives it a human action.
slides.hint: Can the moon really smile? Who smiles?
slides.notes: Sayable: Which one is BEST? Whole-class fingers 1/2/3 before reveal. Contrast: not simile — no like/as. [PRACTISE]
slides.prompt: The moon smiles at me. Which tool is BEST?

slides.feedback: The poet compares running to the wind with like.
slides.hint: Find the word like. What two things are compared?
slides.notes: Sayable: Which one is BEST? Counter wind-confusion: Who runs? The brother — a person. The tool here is like. Not personification. [PRACTISE]
slides.prompt: My brother runs like the wind. Which tool is BEST?

slides.feedback: The word run is repeated on purpose for effect.
slides.hint: How many times do you see run?
slides.notes: Sayable: Which one is BEST? Contrast: no comparison, no non-human action. Keep same 3 choices for predictability. Total Beat 9 ~4 min. Bridge: Now use real noticing. [PRACTISE]
slides.prompt: Run, run, run! Which tool is BEST?

slides.hint: See shoes, sky, windows. Hear rain, voices, bells?
slides.notes: Sayable: Do not invent a new world. Tell me what is really here. Build bank publicly from pupil words (6–8: wet shoes, grey sky, noisy rain, cold floor, umbrellas, dripping bags, sleepy students, water on window). Accept feelings — sleepy, lonely — especially 1E emotion bridge (affirm feeling-subjects miss/love). Volume of concrete nouns/verbs matters, not poetic quality. Keep bank visible into next beat. Bridge: Now use these words. [ELICIT ~5 min]
slides.prompt: Turn on your poetry camera. What do you notice?
slides.stimulus: A rainy school afternoon. SEE — What can you see? HEAR — What can you hear? FEEL — What can you feel? NOTICE — What small thing?

items: The rain taps on the window
The rain taps on the window like tiny fingers.
It waits. It listens. Then it disappears.
slides.notes: Sayable staged: What does the rain do? (verb: taps / knocks / sings, 1E choose) Where? What does it sound like? (It sounds like ___. Tiny fingers? Small drums?) If rain were a person — waits? listens? watches? Title decided aloud: Rain (one word). Load-bearing line verbatim: This is not a perfect poem. It is a poem because we made choices — specific verb, simile, human action, line breaks. Accept variant verbs. Leave visible into next beat as confidence anchor; remove before Beat 15 so nobody copies. [MODEL ~5 min]
slides.prompt: Let's write a poem together. What does the rain do?

slides.hint: Which one can you see right now? Outside, bag, home?
slides.notes: Sayable: You only need ONE subject. Point to it now. Visible commitment in 60 seconds (finger on choice / whisper to neighbour). Steer strugglers to RAIN / SCHOOL / MOON (banked language exists). 1E emotion bridge: pupils choosing SOMETHING I MISS / LOVE — affirm feeling-subjects as valid poem material. Bridge: Here is a recipe if you need steps. [COMMIT ~2 min]
slides.prompt: Choose ONE thing for your poem. Point to it now.
slides.stimulus: RAIN · MY FRIEND · MY PHONE · FOOTBALL · MY CAT / DOG · SCHOOL · THE MOON · A PLACE I LIKE · SOMETHING I MISS · SOMETHING I LOVE · Or your own.

slides.hint: Skip a line if you need to. Keep 6 to 8 lines.
slides.notes: Sayable: A simple recipe — training wheels, not rules. Read once aloud; point to toolbox links (line 5 = simile, line 6 = personification, line 7 = repetition). Reassure: You do not have to use every line exactly. Do NOT collect writing yet. 2E preview not needed for 1E. Single-slide recipe kept after fit check at 1280x665; split only if browser verify overflows. Bridge: Plan in 30 seconds, then write. [REFERENCE ~3 min]
slides.prompt: A simple recipe — training wheels. You need 6 to 8 lines.
slides.text: Line 1: Introduce it. Line 2: What does it look like? Line 3: What does it do? Line 4: What sound, feel, smell? Line 5: Compare it with like or as. Line 6: Give it a human action. Line 7: Repeat a word. Line 8: End with a strong picture.

slides.hint: Stuck? Steal cold, window, grey — then change one word.
slides.notes: Sayable: Copy the frames. Use your own words. Thirty seconds. Model with rain in 60s max, then pupils fill silently. Circulate: first check = subject + one notice. Hard stop at 2 min. Frames: My subject / 3 notices / verb / comparison (It is like ___) / human action (It ___). Bridge: Now write. Six to eight lines. [PLAN ~2 min]
slides.prompt: Plan in 30 seconds. Fill this for YOUR subject.
slides.stimulus: My subject: ___ 3 things I notice: ___ / ___ / ___ One verb: ___ Like: It is like ___. Action: It ___. Example — rain / cold, window, grey / tap / tiny fingers / waits.

slides.notes: Sayable: Start now. One subject. Your choices. 8-min hard stop (timer). Circulate priority: one clear subject → lines appearing → one concrete detail → one tool. Rescue ladder voiceable: What can you see? What does it do? What does it sound like? What is it like? If it were a person, what would it do? Non-starters: point to Beat 14 frames, dictate starter (My ___ ...). Remove Beat 11 model from view. 1E early-finish extension only: Repeat your best line once more. Do NOT heavily correct grammar. Evidence: titled 6–8 line poem. [APPLY ~8 min]
slides.prompt: Write your first poem — about ONE thing. Start now.
slides.task: Write 6–8 lines with a title. Use specific details and one tool. No rhyme needed.

slides.hint: Point to your weakest line. Add one specific word.
slides.notes: Sayable: Do not ask, Is it perfect? Ask, Which line can I make better? 3 min: 1 min check, 2 min rewrite one line. Affirm revisions adding specificity/tool even if grammar imperfect. Descriptive improvement language only, never public marks. Bridge: So what IS poetry, after doing it? [REVISE ~3 min]
slides.prompt: Read your poem like a poet. Improve ONE line.
slides.text: Title. 6–8 lines. Specific words. One poetry tool. I can picture it. I chose line ends.

slides.feedback: Poetry is not difficult English. Poetry is making choices.
slides.hint: Did your poem need big words? Did it need rhyme?
slides.notes: Sayable: Think about your poem. Which one is BEST? Expect C; if A/B replay evidence (comes/feet did not rhyme; cold/taps were not hard). Follow-up oral: What is one choice you made? (simile / strong verb / repeated word / line break) — take 3 answers. Bridge: One last challenge — prove it in two lines. [CONSOLIDATE ~2 min]
slides.prompt: So… what is poetry? Which one is BEST?

slides.hint: Try: The moon ___ . Watches, smiles, waits — or like a lamp.
slides.notes: Sayable: Write two lines now. Use one choice from your toolbox. Take 3–4 shares; for each ask class: What choice did the writer make? Reward any real choice — human action, comparison, strong break — not one perfect answer. Possibles: The moon / watches me. OR The bright moon hangs / like a lamp in the sky. Do NOT judge beautiful. Final line: You have written a poem. Collect exit lines + Beat 15 poems as evidence. [TRANSFER ~2 min]
slides.prompt: Turn this into TWO poetic lines. Use one tool.

title: Poetry Is Easier Than You Think — 1E
